nameStory: This charming flower gets its name from its six-pointed white star shape, which reminded people of the biblical Star of Bethlehem that guided the wise men. According to folklore, the plant originally sprang from fragments of that very star when it fell to Earth. Some of its other nicknames like 'eleven-o'clock lady' and 'nap-at-noon' come from its habit of opening its flowers late in the day and closing them during bright midday sun.
description: Common star-of-Bethlehem is a small spring wildflower that grows from an underground bulb, reaching about 4-12 inches tall. It produces clusters of grass-like leaves at its base and sends up slender stems topped with bright white, six-petaled flowers arranged in a star pattern. Originally from Europe and North Africa, this plant has escaped from gardens throughout New England and now grows wild in many areas. Despite its delicate appearance, it's quite hardy and can form large colonies over time.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant white flowers with six pointed petals arranged in a perfect star shape, about 1 inch across. Each petal has a distinctive green stripe on the underside that's visible when flowers are closed or viewed from below.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge directly from the ground in small tufts. The leaves are smooth to the touch with a prominent white stripe running down the center of each blade.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that forms small clumps from underground bulbs. Multiple flower stems rise above the basal rosette of leaves, each topped with 5-20 flowers in a flat-topped cluster.

idTips.label: Timing Behavior
idTips.description: Flowers have a unique daily rhythm - they stay closed during bright midday sun and open in late afternoon or on cloudy days. This sleepy behavior is quite noticeable and distinctive.

habitat: Look for star-of-Bethlehem in disturbed areas, old gardens, roadsides, fields, and woodland edges throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. Often found near abandoned homesites or spreading from cultivated areas into adjacent wild spaces.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming time from April through May, with white star-shaped flowers opening on warm afternoons. Grass-like leaves emerge early and are most prominent during flowering season.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and leaves begin to yellow and die back by mid-summer. Small seed capsules may be visible on spent flower stems.
seasonality.fall: Plant goes completely dormant with no visible above-ground parts. Underground bulbs are developing energy stores for next spring's growth.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with bulbs resting underground. No visible parts above ground during winter months.

funFact: Leonardo da Vinci included star-of-Bethlehem flowers in several of his paintings, and scientists have used his detailed botanical illustrations to help identify the exact species he observed over 500 years ago!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with wild garlic or other spring bulbs, but star-of-Bethlehem lacks any onion smell when crushed and has that telltale white stripe down each leaf center. The six-pointed star flowers with green stripes on the back are also unique among early spring wildflowers.
contextualKnowledge: While beautiful, star-of-Bethlehem contains toxic compounds and should never be eaten, despite being used in some traditional cuisines. It's considered mildly invasive in North America since it can spread aggressively from bulbs and displace native spring wildflowers.
compareHints: Drooping star-of-Bethlehem, its close relative, has larger flowers that hang downward rather than facing upward, and typically blooms earlier in the season. Common star-of-Bethlehem's upward-facing flowers in flat-topped clusters and later bloom time make it easy to distinguish from its drooping cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Drooping star-of-Bethlehem is distinguished from common star-of-Bethlehem by its hanging, bell-shaped flowers versus the upward-facing, flat, star-shaped flowers of its relative.
